title: Transcript Quantification
text: For transcript quantification, again there are several tools that can be used. Some tools require transcript identification first (FLAIR), but there are many others that can work directly from mapped reads. During this session we will take a look at Bambu, a tool for quantifying reads on a transcript or gene level.

title: Transcript Quantification
text:
Bambu
In some cases, we specifically want to get counts per gene for a version of an annotation, without looking for new isoforms or transcripts. Though Bambu is capable of also identifying new isoforms and transcripts, it is mainly used with organisms that already have a high quality annotation. To able to do this, we again need the mapped reads, a genome sequence and a genome annotation.
Bambu is based within R, a popular programming language used in bioinformatics. Bambu requires one of the latest versions of R, which we have installed for you on the server.


 Disclaimer:

For this course, no prior experience with R or programming is required. You will be able to follow along by simply copying and pasting the commands provided into R. We will focus on understanding what the commands do and how to interpret the results, rather than on learning how to write code from scratch.
That said, if you are interested in working with transcriptomics data, learning R is worthwhile. R is one of the most widely used programming languages for analysing biological data, and it is particularly useful for data analysis and data visualization.
If you are interested in getting started with R, we would also recommend taking a look at RStudio. RStudio provides a user-friendly graphical interface for working with R. It makes programming much more accessible by allowing you to write and organize scripts, run individual commands, view plots, and inspect your data, all within one interface.
Unfortunately, we will not be using RStudio during this course. We are running a specific version of R on a remote server, and the RStudio interface is not currently available for this version of R. Instead, we will work directly with R and use the commands provided throughout the course. This is perfectly sufficient for following the exercises and completing the analyses covered in the course. Click here to take a look at the Rstudio interface.
If you are interested in learning R and would like to join a course that will teach you how to use R from the very beginning, please contact the Bioinformatics Core at the DRP-HCB.

R runs from your current working directory, meaning it has access to the data within that folder and will write any output files to that folder.
Start R by running the following command in the terminal.
/library/training/LRT_Tool/R-4.6.0/bin/R
The Bambu package needs to be installed within R. Note: You won’t need to run this when working on the server.
BiocManager::install("bambu")
Once packages are installed, they still need to activated.
library(bambu)
The command below lists all of the input files for bambu by looking for files ending with pacbio.chromosome2.bam. Multiple samples can be loaded at the same time and the larger the number of samples, the longer the process will take. Running bambu on a server is advised to speed up this process.
files <- list.files(path="./", pattern="pacbio.chromosome2.bam$")


 Challenge:

How many files have we prepared for Bambu?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Don’t worry if you don’t know how to use R. To get the values within a variable in R, just type its name and press enter.
files



We can run bambu with a single command. Bambu first prepares the annotation for efficient access. If you use the genome often, the annotation can be prepared beforehand and saved into an R object to save time.
se <- bambu(reads = files, annotations = "../GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14_genomic.gtf", genome = "../GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14_genomic.fna", ncore = 5, discovery = FALSE)
Note: This will take several minutes.
Once bambu has finished, we can write the output to a folder named bambu.
writeBambuOutput(se, path = "./bambu/")
Open up a new terminal to take a look at the resulting files. We want to keep the R session running to be able to continue working with the data later on.
Several files are generated, the most important are the files starting with counts. Bambu generates files for both transcript level and gene level. Depending on the analysis, either file can be used.


 Challenge:

How many transcripts have been reported? And how many genes?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Remember that we can check how many lines a file has with wc -l.
wc -l counts_transcript.txt

wc -l counts_gene.txt



Bambu has the functionality to visualise genes, the different transcripts found for a gene, and the per sample read counts for each transcript. This can help you to visualise specific transcripts that are being used differently between sample groups. Because we are working on the command line, we cannot directly see the plots, however we can easily save them to a pdf file.
pdf("UGP2.pdf")
plotBambu(se, type = "annotation", gene_id = "UGP2")
dev.off()
The plot is saved to the current working directory. View the plot in your web directory or view the prepared version below.



Bambu visualisation of UGP2 gene




 Challenge:

How many transcripts have been reported for UGP2?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

The top of the image shows the different transcripts available for the gene.



Bambu also has options to create other plots like PCA and heatmaps.
Because we have data for all samples using PacBio, Nanopore Direct sequencing and Nanopore RNA sequencing, we have prepared a set of data which contain the results for all samples using bambu.
To load the data into R, run the following command.
seall <- readRDS(file="bamburesults_allsamples.rds")
To create a pca plot which shows information on groups, group information needs to be added to the R object that we want to look at. Within bambu, information of samples is captured in colData(seall).


 Challenge:

Run colData(seall) in R.
What information is currently available for the samples?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

The only information currently available is the names of the samples.



There are several ways to add data, for now we will add data manually. This is normally not recommended, as mistakes are easily made, but for this example it will do.
colData(seall)$seqtype <- c("direct", "nanopore", "pacbio","direct", "nanopore", "pacbio","direct", "nanopore", "pacbio","direct", "nanopore", "pacbio","direct", "nanopore", "pacbio","direct", "nanopore", "pacbio","direct", "nanopore", "pacbio","direct", "nanopore", "pacbio")
Now, let’s create a pca plot.
pdf("pcaseall.pdf")
plotBambu(seall, type="pca", "seqtype")
dev.off()
View the plot in your web folder or view a prepared version below.



PCA plot of all samples from different sequencing types




 Challenge:

Is there anything that stands out to you from the pca plot?

title: Long Read Transcriptomics
text:
Welcome to our Long Read Transcriptomics course. This course is hosted by the Bioinformatics Core at the DRP-HCB.
During this course you will learn to:
During this course, we will work through the following workflow and explain the process, different steps to take depending on the data that we have, and talk about things to watch out.

title: Transcript Identification
text:
Identifying novel transcripts is an important step in transcriptome analysis, particularly for non-model organisms. Several tools are available to identify transcripts that are not present in existing annotations.
A comparative study cited in the references evaluates the performance of different tools and provides recommendations on their suitability for different applications. Among the tools assessed, FLAIR performs well across a broad range of applications, making it a useful choice for both model and non-model organisms. Therefore, in this training, we will use FLAIR to identify novel transcripts.
Other options include (IsoQuant and TALON.

title: Transcript Identification
text:
FLAIR
To annotate transcripts, FLAIR requires mapped reads in BAM format. FLAIR is one of the few tools that can evaluate on a per sample basis and then merge the results. This is especially useful if computational resources are limited or samples are added after the initial analysis.
We will run this analysis on our PacBio data. However, the steps are exactly the same for Nanopore reads.

Sample Transcript Identification
Before we start, the BAM file needs to be indexed.
samtools index H146_pacbio.chromosome2.bam
This will generate an index file for the BAM file. The index file is used by different tools to access data within the BAM file more efficiently. Once the index file has been generated, transcript identification can be performed.
flair transcriptome -g GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14_genomic.fna -f GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14_genomic.gtf -t 5 -b H146_pacbio.chromosome2.bam -o H146_pacbio.chromosome2
The file GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14_genomic.gtf is the annotation file. This contains existing transcript annotations for the human genome.
Note: This will take about 5 minutes.
Several files are generated, in this case the most important ones are the ones ending in .bed, .fa and read.map.txt.


 Challenge:

Take a look at the bed file. How many annotations are there within the file? How many of these are new?
Hint: New annotations are labelled with the ID of the sample. In this case the ID is SRR30947496.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

First, to check the number of annotations in the file, we can use wc
wc -l H146_pacbio.chromosome2.isoforms.bed
To check which annotations are new, aka contain the SRR30947496 label, we can use grep
grep "SRR30947496" H146_pacbio.chromosome2.isoforms.bed | wc -l



A large number of sample specific novel transcripts have been identified. Let’s look at what happens if we merge results from multiple samples.


Merge Transcripts
The data for multiple samples has been prepared for you in the combine folder.
cd combine
Within this folder, there is a manifest file which is needed to combine the different samples.
less pacbio_manifest.txt
The file contains information on the samples to merge and the corresponding flair output files from the previous step. The combine step uses these files to look at how reads are mapped against the reference genome, the sequences of the transcripts and the annotation they align to on the reference genome. Once everything is in place, the files can be merged.
flair combine -c -m pacbio_manifest.txt -o pacbio_merge
Take a look at the files generated.


 Challenge:

Take a look at the output bed file. How many annotations are there within the file? How does this compare to the number in the per sample annotation?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

To check the number of annotations in the file, we can use wc
wc -l pacbio_merge.bed



The number of annotation is greatly decreased compared to the per sample annotation.


 Challenge:

Can you think of reasons why the number of annotations has decreased?

There are three main reasons why the number of annotations has changed:

Annotations have been merged into a single transcript, because reads of other samples compliment our original sample, overlapping and generating a single transcript from multiple.
Transcripts have only been found in a single sample with a low number of reads covering it, meaning it might be an incorrect annotation. The thresholds for this can be adjusted in the combine command.
The transcript is too short for it to be considered a true gene. Again this can be adjusted in the combine command.

The completed genome annotation is available in both bed and gtf format, the files most often used by quantification methods. Be aware that this annotation might not include all isoforms available, but isoforms that have been found within this set of samples. The annotation can be updated as more samples become available.
In case there are specific samples you are interested in, each sample can be explored individually.
You might have noticed that both flair commands generate a count file as well. This is the quantification of each transcript within the annotation and these files can be used for downstream analysis. We will also take a look at how to quantify reads without identification first.

title: Quality Control
text: As long-read sequencing has become more affordable and widely accessible, transcriptomics has emerged as one of the key fields to benefit from this technology. The option to sequence full-length transcripts provides a clear view of transcript structure, alternative splicing, and the complexity of gene expression. In this session, we will learn to identify novel transcripts, quantify gene expression in both model and non model organisms, and discuss the differences between Nanopore and PacBio sequencing.

text:

title: Quality Control
text:
Data
We will begin by looking at Nanopore and PacBio sequencing performed on the same samples. The raw data comes from the following publication:
Benchmarking long-read RNA-sequencing technologies with LongBench: A cross-platform reference dataset profiling cancer cell lines with bulk and single-cell approaches
Move into your workshop directory.
cd ~/long_read_transcriptomics
The following commands will copy the data into this folder if you are on the DRP-HCB bioinformatics server.
cp -R /library/training/ASD/04_LRT/data ./LRT
If you are working on another computer or server, you can download the data as a tar.gz file and extract it using the following commands.
## No need to run this if working on the DRP-HCB bioinformatics server
wget https://bifx-core3.bio.ed.ac.uk/training/ASD/LRT.tar.gz
tar -xzvf LRT.tar.gz

title: Quality Control
text:
PacBio
PacBio is a long read sequencing technology that uses a single molecule real-time (SMRT) sequencing approach. This allows for the generation of long reads, which can be used to sequence full-length transcripts.

Quality control
Because PacBio reads are long, sequencing short transcripts can be inefficient. To overcome this, PacBio uses a method called the Kinnex protocol, which joins multiple transcripts together to create longer reads. This maximises the sequencing output but can make downstream processing more complex. In most cases the data which we get from a provider is separated into separate transcripts, however confirming this has happened is important.
cd LRT

NanoPlot -t 8 --ubam hifi_reads.bcM0002_200K.bam --plot dots -o NanoPlot_hifi
Navigate to your web directory to view the results. Alternatively, you can look at this pre-generated Nanoplot report.


 Challenge:

Take a look at the NanoPlot results. How does the average length of the reads compare to average transcript length?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

On average, the length of transcript sequences is around 2kb for humans. The average of the reads here is 16kb, much larger than expected.



PacBio has an optimal read length of around 18kb. If your average read lengths are close to this, then most likely the data is still joined together. We can use a tool called skera to separate transcripts by searching for the adapter sequences between them. These adapters are stored in a FASTA file and can be downloaded from the PacBio website. The adapters are already available to you in the file mas8.fasta.
less mas8.fasta
skera split hifi_reads.bcM0002_200K.bam mas8.fasta segmented.bam
Run NanoPlot again to see what effect this has on the reads.
NanoPlot -t 8 --ubam segmented.bam --plot dots -o NanoPlot_segmented
View the results in your web directory or here.


 Challenge:

How have the results changed?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

On average, the length of transcript sequences is now 2k, which is expected for this sample. The total number of reads has gone up, because the reads have been split into multiple sections.



Whether the Kinnex protocol was used or not, the reads will contain primer sequences which need to be removed before the data can be used for downstream analysis. The primer sequences typically contain sequencing adapters and sequencing barcodes used to identify samples.
We will use a tool called lima to remove the adapters and separate samples by barcode. The sequencing primers can be found in isoseq.fasta and are specific to this sequencing protocol. If you have your own data, check which primers and barcodes have been used.
less isoseq.fasta
lima segmented.bam isoseq.fasta segmented.fl.bam --isoseq --peek-guess
If the sequencing library contains multiple samples, lima will separate the reads into different file sets. In this case, there is only one sample, and therefore only one set of files is generated.


 Challenge:

Take a look at the files generated. Which file contains our reads?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

ls
There are a number of files generated, including a report of the results. The reads for our sample are in segmented.fl.IsoSeqX_bc02_5p--IsoSeqX_3p.bam. The naming of the file reflects the name of the primers or barcodes within the fasta file used during lima.



The final preparation step is to perform a refinement. This makes sure all of the reads have been properly separated, have their primers removed and if applicable can check if reads have a polyA tail and remove this from the reads.
isoseq refine segmented.fl.IsoSeqX_bc02_5p--IsoSeqX_3p.bam isoseq.fasta segmented.refined.bam --require-polya


Mapping to a reference genome
In order to identify and quantify isoforms, the reads first need to be mapped to a reference genome. For long reads, the best mapper is minimap2. PacBio has its own implementation of minimap2, named pbmm2, which is optimised for PacBio. However, in this case, we will use the base version of minimap2.
Minimap2 requires reads in a fastq file, so we first need to transform our data to fastq format.
samtools bam2fq segmented.refined.bam | pigz -c > segmented.refined.fastq.gz
We use samtools bam2fq to convert the bam file to fastq format, and pigz to compress the output. Once the reads are in fastq format, minimap2 can map them to the reference genome.
minimap2 -t 5 -a -x splice:hq -s 40 -G 350k --MD --secondary=no GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14_genomic.fna segmented.refined.fastq.gz | samtools view -hb - | samtools sort - > refined.mapped.bam
Here we provide GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14_genomic.fna as the reference, which is the human genome assembly GRCh38.p14. The -x parameter tells minimap2 which type of reads we are mapping, in this case splice:hq is used for high quality PacBio spliced reads. You can explore the other input options to minimap2 by typing minimap2 --help. The output of minimap2 is piped to samtools view to convert the output to bam format, and then piped to samtools sort to sort the reads by their position in the genome. The final output is written to refined.mapped.bam.
Note: This will take some time, for today it can be skipped if it takes too long, data has been prepared for you for next steps.
At this point, the PacBio data is ready for downstream processing, whether that is identification of new isoforms and genes or quantification of transcripts. We will get into both of these applications in the next session.

title: Quality Control
text:
NanoPore
Before we continue processing the data, let’s take a look at the NanoPore sequencing and the different steps involved in pre-processing. Nanopore has two different methods for generating reads for the transcriptome. The first method transforms the RNA into cDNA and uses PCR to add adapters to the reads. The second method takes the RNA as is, attaches an adapter by ligation, and is sequenced on a specific RNA flowcell. Both methods have their pros and cons, and in terms of processing, these differ slightly when it comes to mapping the reads, which we will get into later. However, the pre-processing is the same between the two methods. The data for NanoPore for both methods will be reported in BAM or FASTQ format. Either of these can be checked with NanoPlot.
NanoPlot -t 8 --fastq nanopore.fastq.gz --plot dots -o NanoPlot_nanopore
The results can be viewed in your web directory or here.


 Challenge:

Take a look at the results generated and compare to the PacBio results. How do the results differ?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

The Nanopore sequencing is already in line with the expected lengths for transcripts. The average quality of reads is lower compared to PacBio. There is more variation in lengths found.



Depending on the results and species that is being sequenced, we might want to perform quality filtering. If there are multiple species within the sample, especially if those species are closely related, removing low quality reads can improve the results.
Sequencing data that is above a Phred quality score of 20 is considered to be high quality. With Nanopore this is often not reached, so to keep the data of high quality but not lose too much data, the cutoff is often set to the mean read quality. In this case the mean quality is 12, using nanoq we can filter out anything below that threshold.
nanoq --min-qual 12 -i nanopore.fastq.gz -o nanopore.trimmed.fastq.gz
Nanoq will report how many reads are left after filtering and the general statistics on the resulting reads. This includes the following: Number of reads, number of bases, N50, longest read, shortest read, mean length, median length, mean quality and median quality. The data is now ready for mapping.
To check the results, run NanoPlot on the trimmed results.
NanoPlot -t 8 --fastq nanopore.trimmed.fastq.gz --plot dots -o NanoPlot_trimmed
View the report in your web directory or here.
Finally, similar to PacBio, the reads need to be mapped against the reference genome. Again we can use minimap2, but the command is slightly different. In this case, we are mapping RNA reads, so we use splice. The -uf parameter tells minimap2 that the reads are from a direct RNA sequencing experiment.
minimap2 -t 5 -a -x splice -s 40 -G 350k -uf --MD --secondary=no GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14_genomic.fna nanopore.trimmed.fastq.gz | samtools view -hb - | samtools sort - > nanopore.mapped.bam
Once mapped, the data is ready for transcript identification and quantification.

title: Summary
text:
This summary should help you decide which steps are necessary for you to start analysing your data. The most important considerations before you start are the platform used for sequencing reads and quality and completeness of your reference genome.
Processing PacBio data is generally more involved than processing Nanopore data. However, PacBio data typically generates higher read quality, which can be beneficial for downstream analyses, especially if you are working with an unknown species. You can inspect the NanoPlot quality control reports to check whether Kinnex was used and whether the data has already undergone preprocessing when looking at PacBio. Whether using PacBio or Nanopore, these reports are useful to understand the data that you are working and the impact the quality of the reads will have on downstream results.
If you are working with a well-annotated genome, such as a model organism, or with a genome that has some basic annotation available but where the annotations have not been experimentally or independently validated and are likely to be incomplete.
If your genome does not have any annotation at all, doing a genome annotation using a tool such as BRAKER3 can be extremely valuable. This will provide an initial set of predicted genes and transcripts, giving you a starting point for downstream analyses.
